fabian.etymology: L. Fabianus, Fabius, belonging to Fabius.

fable.etymology: F., fr. L. fabula, fr. fari to speak, say. See Ban, and cf. Fabulous, Fame.

fabric.etymology: L. fabrica fabric, workshop: cf. F. fabrique fabric. See Forge.

fabricate.etymology: L. fabricatus, p.p. of fabricari, fabricare, to frame, build, forge, fr. fabrica. See Fabric, Farge.

fabulist.etymology: Cf. F. fabuliste, fr. L. fabula. See Fable.

fabulous.etymology: L. fabulosus; cf. F. fabuleux. See Fable.

facade.etymology: F., fr. It. facciata, fr. fassia face, L. facies. See Face.

face.etymology: F., from L. facies form, shape, face, perh. from facere to make (see Fact); or perh. orig. meaning appearance, and from a root meaning to shine, and akin to E. fancy. Cf. Facetious.

facet.etymology: F. facette, dim. of face face. See Face.

facial.etymology: LL. facialis, fr. L. facies face : cf. F. facial.

facile.etymology: L. facilis, prop., capable of being done or made, hence, facile, easy, fr. facere to make, do: cf. F. facile. Srr Fact, and cf. Faculty.

facility.etymology: L. facilitas, fr. facilis easy: cf. F. facilitFacile.

facsimile.etymology: L. fac simile make like; or an abbreviation of factum simile made like; facere to make + similes like. See Fact, and Simile.

fact.etymology: L. factum, fr. facere to make or do. Cf. Feat, Affair, Benefit, Defect, Fashion, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

faction.etymology: L. factio a doing, a company of persons acting together, a faction: cf. F. faction See Fashion.

factitious.etymology: L. factitius, fr. facere to make. See Fact, and cf. Fetich.

factor.etymology: L. factor a doer: cf. F. facteur a factor. See Fact.

factotum.etymology: L., do everything; facere to do + totus all : cf. F. factotum. See Fact, and Total.

facultative.etymology: L. facultas, -atis, faculty: cf. F. facultatif, G. fakultativ.

faculty.etymology: F. facult, L. facultas, fr. facilis easy (cf. facul easily), fr. fecere to make. See Fact, and cf. Facility.

fade.etymology: F., prob. fr. L. vapidus vapid, or possibly fr,fatuus foolish, insipid.

fag.etymology: Cf. LG. fakk wearied, weary, vaak slumber, drowsiness, OFries. fai, equiv. to fach devoted to death, OS. f, OHG. feigi, G. feig, feige, cowardly, Icel. feigr fated to die, AS. f, Scot. faik, to fail, stop, lower the price; or perh. the same word as E. flag to droop.

fagot.etymology: F., prob. aug. of L. fax, facis, torch, perh. orig., a bundle of sticks; cf. Gr. Fagotto.

faience.etymology: F., fr. Faenza, a town in Italy, the original place of manufacture.

fail.etymology: F. failir, fr. L. fallere, falsum, to deceive, akin to E. fall. See Fail, and cf. Fallacy, False, Fault.

fain.etymology: OE. fain, fagen, AS. fægen; akin to OS. fagan, Icel. faginn glad; AS. fægnian to rejoice, OS. faganon, Icel. fagna, Goth. faginon, cf. Goth. faheds joy; and fr. the same root as E. fair. Srr Fair, a., and cf. Fawn to court favor.

faineant.etymology: F.; fait he does + néant nothing.

faint.etymology: OE. faint, feint, false, faint, F. feint, p.p. of feindre to feign, suppose, hesitate. See Faign, and cf. Feint.

fair.etymology: OE. fair, fayer, fager, AS. fæger; akin to OS. & OHG. fagar, Isel. fagr, Sw. fager, Dan. faver, Goth. fagrs fit, also to E. fay, G. fügen, to fit. fegen to sweep, cleanse, and prob. also to E. fang, peace, pact, Cf. Fang, Fain, Fay to fit.

fairy.etymology: OE. fairie, faierie, enchantment, fairy folk, fairy, OF. faerie enchantment, F. féer, fr. LL. Fata one of the goddesses of fate. See Fate, and cf. Fay a fairy.

faith.etymology: OE. feith, fayth, fay, OF. feid, feit, fei, F. foi, fr. L. fides; akin to fidere to trust, Gr. th is perhaps due to the influence of such words as truth, health, wealth. See Bid, Bide, and cf. Confide, Defy, Fealty.

fake.etymology: Cf. Scot. faik fold, stratum of stone, AS. fæc space, interval, G. fach compartment, partition, row, and E. fay to fit.

falcate.etymology: L. falcatus, fr. falx, falcis, a sickle or scythe.

falchion.etymology: OE. fauchon, OF. fauchon, LL. fälcio, fr. L. falx, falcis, a sickle, cf. Gr. falcon; cf. It. falcione. Cf. Defalcation.

falciform.etymology: L. falx, falcis, a sickle + -form: cf. F. falciforme.

falcon.etymology: OE. faucon, faucoun, OF. faucon, falcon, faucon, fr. LL. falco, perh. from L. falx, falcis, a sickle or scythe, and named from its curving talons. Cf. Falchion.

falconer.etymology: OE. fauconer, OF. falconier, fauconier, F. fauconnier. See Falcon.

fall.etymology: AS. feallan; akin to D. vallen, OS. & OHG. fallan, G. fallen, Icel. Falla, Sw. falla, Dan. falde, Lith. pulti, L. fallere to deceive, Gr. sfa`llein to cause to fall, Skr. sphal, sphul, to tremble. Cf. Fail, Fell, v. t., to cause to fall.

fallacious.etymology: L. fallaciosus, fr. fallacia: cf. F. fallacieux. See Fallacy.

fallacy.etymology: OE. fallace, fallas, deception, F. fallace, fr. L. fallacia, fr. fallax deceitful, deceptive, fr. fallere to deceive. See Fail.

fallible.etymology: LL. fallibilis, fr. L. fallere to deceive: cf. F. faillible. See Fail.

fallow.etymology: AS. fealu, fealo, pale yellow or red; akin to D. vaal fallow, faded, OHG. falo, G. falb, fahl, Icel. fölr, and prob. to Lith. palvas, OSlav. plavpallidus pale, pallere to be pale, Gr. palita. Cf. Pale, Favel, a., Favor.

false.etymology: L. falsus, p.p. of fallere to deceive; cf. OF. faus, fals, F. faux, and AS. fals fraud. See Fail, Fall.

roots.meaning: A termination denoting state, condition, quality, character, totality, as in manhood, childhood, knighthood, brotherhood. Sometimes it is written, chiefly in obsolete words, in the form - head.

falsetto.etymology: It. falsetto, dim. fr. L. falsus. See False.

falsify.etymology: L. falsus false + -ly: cf. F. falsifier. See False, a.

roots.meaning: A suffix forming adjectives and adverbs, and denoting likeness or resemblance.

falsity.etymology: L. falsitas: cf. F. fausseté, OF. also, falsité. See False, a.

falter.etymology: OE. falteren, faltren, prob. from fault. See Fault, v. & n.

fame.etymology: OF. fame, L. fama, fr. fari to speak, akin to Gr. Ban, and cf. Fable, Fate, Euphony, Blame.

familiar.etymology: OE. familer, familier, F. familier, fr. L. familiaris, fr. familia family. See Family.

familiarity.etymology: OE. familarite, F. familiaritéfr. L. faniliaritas. See Familiar.

family.etymology: From Late Middle English famylye , from Latin familia ( “ a household ” ) . Displaced native Old English hīred and hād . Doublet of familia .

famine.etymology: F. famine, fr. L. fames hunger; cf. Gr. hani loss, lack, ha to leave.

famish.etymology: OE. famen; cf. OF. afamer, L. fames. See Famine, and cf. Affamish.

famous.etymology: L. famosus, fr. fama fame: cf. F. fameux. See Fame.

fan.etymology: AS. fann, fr. L. vannus fan, van for winnowing grain; cf. F. van. Cf. Van a winnowing machine, Winnow.

fanatic.etymology: L. fanaticus inspired by divinity, enthusiastic, frantic, fr. fanum fane: cf. F. fanatique. See Fane.

fancy.etymology: Contr. fr. fantasy, OF. fantasie, fantaisie, F. fantaisie, L. phantasia, fr. Gr. bhato shine. Cf. Fantasy, Fantasia, Epiphany, Phantom.

fandango.etymology: Sp. A name brought, together with the dance, from the West Indies to Spain.

fang.etymology: OE. fangen, fongen, fon (g orig. only in p.p. and imp. tense), AS. f; akin to D. vangen, OHG. fahan, G. fahen, fangen, Isel. fa, Sw. f, f, Dan. fange, faae, Goth. fahan, and prob. to E. fair, peace, pact. Cf. Fair, a.

farad.etymology: From Michael Faraday, the English electrician.

farce.etymology: F. Farcir, L. farcire; akin to Gr. Force to stuff, Diaphragm, Frequent, Farcy, Farse.

fardel.etymology: OF. fardel, F. fardeau; cf. Sp. fardel, fardillo, fardo, LL. fardellus; prob. fr. Ar. fard one of the two parts of an object divisible into two, hence, one of the two parts of a camel's load. Cf. Furl.

fare.etymology: AS. faran to travel, fare; akin to OS., Goth., & OHG. faran to travel, go, D. varen, G. fahren, OFries., Isel., & Sw. fara, Dan. fare, Gr. peritus experienced, portus port, Skr. par to bring over. sq. root78. Cf Chaffer, Emporium, Far, Ferry, Ford, Peril, Port a harbor, Pore, n.

farina.etymology: L., meal, flour, fr. far a sort of grain, spelt; akin to E. barley.

farm.etymology: OE. ferme rent, lease, F. ferme, LL. firma, fr. L. firmus firm, fast, firmare to make firm or fast. See Firm, a. & n.

faro.etymology: Said to be so called because the Egyptian king Pharaoh was formerly represented upon one of the cards.

farrago.etymology: L. farrago, -aginis, mi8xed fodder for cattle, mash, medley, fr. far a sort of grain. See Farina.

farrier.etymology: OE. farrour, ferrer, OF. ferreor, ferrier, LL. Ferrator, ferrarius equorum, from ferrare to shoe a horse, ferrum a horseshoe, fr. L. ferrum iron. Cf. Ferreous.

farrow.etymology: AS. fearh a little pig; a akin to OHG. farh, farah, pig, dim. farheli little pig, G. fercel, D. varken pig, Lith. parszas OIr. orc,L. porcus, Gr. Pork.

farther.etymology: For farrer, OE. ferrer, compar. of far; confused with further. Cf. Farthest.

farthing.etymology: OE. furthing, AS. feór, fr. feór fourth, feór, feówer, four. See Four.

farthingale.etymology: OE. vardingale, fardingale, fr. OF. vertugale, verdugade, F. vertugade, vertugadin, from Sp. verdugado, being named from its hoops, fr. verdugo a young shoot of tree, fr. verde green, fr. L. viridis. See Verdant.

fascia.etymology: L., a band: cf. It. fascia. See Fasces, and cf. Fess.

fascicle.etymology: L. fasciculus, dim. of fascis. See Fasces.

fashion.etymology: OE. fasoun, facioun, shape, manner, F. facon, orig., a making, fr. L. factio a making, fr. facere to make. See Fact, Feat, and cf. Faction.

fast.etymology: AS. fæstan; akin to D. vasten, OHG. fasten, G. fasten, Icel. & Sw. fasta, Dan. faste, Goth. fastan to keep, observe, fast, and prob. to E. fast firm.

fasten.etymology: AS. fæstnian; akin to OHG. festinon. See Fast, a.

fastidious.etymology: L. fastidiosus disdainful, fr. fastidium loathing, aversion, perh. fr. fastus arrogance (of uncertain origin) + taedium loathing. Cf. Tedious, Fash.

fastigiate.etymology: L. fastigium gable end, top, height, summit.

fastness.etymology: AS. fæstnes, fr. fæst fast. See Fast, a.

fatal.etymology: L. fatalis, fr. fatum: cf. F. fatal. See Fate.

fate.etymology: L. fatum a prophetic declaration, oracle, what is ordained by the gods, destiny, fate, fr. fari to speak: cf. OF. fat. See Fame, Fable, Ban, and cf. 1st Fay, Fairy.

father.etymology: OE. fader, AS. fæder; akin to OS. fadar, D. vader, OHG. fatar, G. vater, Icel. Fa Sw. & Dan. fader, OIr. athir, L. pater, Gr. pitr, perh. fr. Skr. pa protect. Papa, Paternal, Patriot, Potential, Pablum.

fatherland.etymology: Imitated fr. D. vaderland. See Father, and Land.

fatigue.etymology: F., fr. fatiguer to fatigue, L. fatigare; cf. L. affatim sufficiently.

fatuity.etymology: L. fatuitas, fr. fatuus foolish: cf. F. fatuité Cf. Fatuous.

faucet.etymology: F. fausset, perh. fr. L. fauces throat.

fault.etymology: OE. faut, faute, F. faute (cf. It., Sp., & Pg. falta), fr. a verb meaning to want, fail, freq., fr. L. fallere to deceive. See Fail, and cf. Default.

faun.etymology: L. Faunus, fr. favere to be favorable. See Favor.

fauna.etymology: NL.: cf. F. faune. See Faun.

favorable.etymology: F. favorable, L. favorabilis favored, popular, pleasing, fr. favor. See Favor, n.

favorite.etymology: OF. favorit favored, F. favori, fem. favorite, p.p. of OF. favorir, cf. It. favorito, frm. favorita, fr. favorire to favor. See Favor.

fawn.etymology: OF. faon the young one of any beast, a fawn, F. faon a fawn, for fedon, fr. L. fetus. See Fetus.

fay.etymology: F. fée. See Fate, and cf. Fairy.

fealty.etymology: OE. faute, OF. fauté, fealté, feelé, feelteit, fr. L. fidelitas, fr. fidelis faithful. See Feal, and cf. Fidelity.

fear.etymology: OE. fer, feer, fere, AS. f a coming suddenly upon, fear, danger; akin to D. vaar, OHG. fara danger, G. gefahr, Icel. far harm, mischief, plague, and to E. fare, peril. See Fare.

feasible.etymology: F. faisable, fr. faire to make or do, fr. L. facere. See Fact, Feat.

feast.etymology: OE. feste festival, holiday, feast, OF. feste festival, F. fête, fr. L. festum, pl. festa, fr. festus joyful, festal; of uncertain origin. Cf. Fair, n., Festal, F.

feat.etymology: OE. fet, OF. fet, fait, F. fait, factum, fr. L. facere, factum, to make or do. Cf. Fact, Feasible, Do.

feather.etymology: OE. fether, AS. fe; akin to D. veder, OHG. fedara, G. feder, Icel. fjö, Sw. fjäder, Dan. fjæder, Gr. pattra wing, feathr, pat to fly, and prob. to L. penna feather, wing. sq. root76, 248. Cf. Pen a feather.

feature.etymology: OE. feture form, shape, feature, OF. faiture fashion, make, fr. L. factura a making, formation, fr. facere, factum, to make. See Feat, Fact, and cf. Facture.

febrifuge.etymology: L. febris fever + fugare to put to flight, from fugere to flee: cf. F. fébrifuge. see Febrile, Feverfew.

febrile.etymology: F. fébrile, from L. febris fever. See Fever.

february.etymology: L. Februarius, orig., the month of expiation, because on the fifteenth of this month the great feast of expiation and purification was held, fr. februa, pl., the Roman festival or purification; akin to februare to purify, expiate.

fecula.etymology: L.fae burnt tartar or salt of tartar, dim. of faex, faecis, sediment, dregs: cf. F. fécule.

feculence.etymology: L. faeculentia dregs, filth: cf. F. féculence.

feculent.etymology: L. faeculentus, fr. faecula: cf. F. féculent. See Fecula.

fecund.etymology: L. fecundus, from the root of fetus: cf. F. fécond. see Fetus.

fecundate.etymology: L. fecundare, fr. fecundus. See Fecund.

fecundity.etymology: L. fecunditas: cf. F. fécondité. See Fecund.

federal.etymology: L. foedus league, treaty, compact; akin to fides faith: cf. F. fédéral. see Faith.

federate.etymology: L. foederatus, p.p. of foederare to establish by treaty or league, fr. foedus. See Federal.

fee.etymology: OE. fe, feh, feoh, cattle, property, money, fiet, AS. feoh cattle, property, money; the senses of "property, money," arising from cattle being used in early times as a medium of exchange or payment, property chiefly consisting of cattle; akin to OS. feuh cattle, property, D. vee cattle, OHG. fihu, fehu, G. vieh, Icel. f cattle, property, money, Goth. faíhu, L. pecus cattle, pecunia property. money, Skr. pa cattle, perh. orig., "a fastened or tethered animal," from a root signifying to bind, and perh. akin to E. fang, fair, a.; cf. OF. fie, flu, feu, fleu, fief, F. fief, from German, of the same origin. the sense fief is due to the French. Feud, Fief, Fellow, Pecuniary.

feeble.etymology: OE. feble, OF. feble, flebe, floibe, floible, foible, F. faible, L. flebilis to be wept over, lamentable, wretched, fr. flere to weep. Cf. Foible.

feed.etymology: AS. f, fr. f food; akin to C. f, OFries f, f, D. voeden, OHG. fuottan, Icel. fæ, Sw. föda, Dan. föde. Food.

feel.etymology: AS. f; akin to OS. gif to perceive, D. voelen to feel, OHG. fuolen, G. fühlen, Icel. falma to grope, and prob. to AS. folm paim of the hand, L. palma. Cf. Fumble, Palm.

feign.etymology: OE. feinen, F. feindre (p. pr. feignant), fr. L. fingere; akin to L. figura figure,and E. dough. See Dough, and cf. Figure, Faint, Effigy, Fiction.

feint.etymology: F. feint, p.p. of feindre to feign. See Feign.

feldspar.etymology: G. feldspath; feld field + spath spar.

felicitate.etymology: L. felicitatus, p.p. of felicitare to felicitate, fr. felix, -icis, happy. See felicity.

felicity.etymology: OE. felicite, F. félicité, fr. L. felicitas, fr. felix, -icis, happy, fruitful; akin to fetus.

feline.etymology: L. felinus, fr. feles, felis, cat, prob. orig., the fruitful: cf. F. félin. See Fetus.

fell.etymology: OE. fel, OF. fel cruel, fierce, perfidious; cf. AS. fel (only in comp.) OF. fel, as a noun also accus. felon, is fr. LL. felo, of unknown origin; cf. Arm fall evil, Ir. feal, Arm. falloni treachery, Ir. & Gael. feall to betray; or cf. OHG. fillan to flay, torment, akin to E. fell skin. Cf. Felon.

fellow.etymology: OE. felawe, felaghe, Icel. felagi, fr. felag companionship, prop., a laying together of property; fe property + lag a laying, pl. lög law, akin to liggja to lie. See Fee, and Law, Lie to be low.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting state, office, dignity, profession, or art; as in lordship, friendship, chancellorship, stewardship, horsemanship.

felly.etymology: OE. feli, felwe, felow, AS. felg, felge; akin to D. velg, G. felge, OHG. felga felly (also, a harrow, but prob. a different word), Dan. felge.

felon.etymology: OE., adj., cruel, n., villain, ruffian, traitor, whitlow, F. félon traitor, in OF. also, villain, fr. LL. felo. See Fell, a.

felony.etymology: OE. felonie cruelty, OF. felonie, F. félonie treachery, malice. See Felon, n.

felt.etymology: AS. felt; akin to D. vilt, G. filz, and possibly to Gr. pilus hair, pileus a felt cap or hat.

felucca.etymology: It. feluca (cf. Sp. faluca, Pg. falua), fr. Ar. fulk ship, or harraqah a sort of ship.

female.etymology: OE. femel, femal, F. femelle, fr. L. femella, dim. of femina woman. See Feminine.

feminine.etymology: L. femininus, fr. femina woman; prob. akin to L. fetus, or to Gr. fæmme woman, maid: cf. F. féminin. See Fetus.

femoral.etymology: L. femur, femoris, thigh: cf. F. fémoral.

fen.etymology: AS. fen, fenn, marsh, mud, dirt; akin to D. veen, OFries. fenne, fene, OHG. fenna, G. fenn, Icel. fen, Goth. fani mud.

fender.etymology: From Fend, v. t. & i., cf. Defender.

fennel.etymology: AS. fenol, finol, from L. feniculum, faeniculum, dim. of fenum, faenum, hay: cf. F. fenouil. Cf. Fenugreek. Finochio.

fenugreek.etymology: L. faenum Graecum, lit., Greek hay: cf. F. fenugrec. Cf. Fennel.

ferial.etymology: LL. ferialis, fr. L. ferie holidays: cf. F. férial. See 5th Fair.

ferine.etymology: L. ferinus, fr. ferus wild. See Fierce.

ferment.etymology: L. fermentum ferment (in senses 1 & 2), perh. for fervimentum, fr. fervere to be boiling hot, boil, ferment: cf. F. ferment. Cf. 1st Barm, Fervent.

ferocious.etymology: L. ferox, -ocis, fierce: cf. F. féroce. See Ferocity.

ferocity.etymology: L. ferocitas, fr. ferox, -ocis, fierce, kin to ferus wild: cf. F. ferocité. See Fierce.

ferret.etymology: F. furet, cf. LL. furo; prob. fr. L. fur thief (cf. Furtive); cf. Arm. fur wise, sly.

ferric.etymology: L. ferrum iron: cf. F. ferrique. See Ferrous.

roots.meaning: A combining form indicating ferric iron as an ingredient; as, ferricyanide.
A prefix, or combining form, indicating ferrous iron as an ingredient; as, ferrocyanide.

ferrule.etymology: Formerly verrel, F. virole, fr. L. viriola little bracelet, dim. of viriae, pl., bracelets; prob. akin to viere to twist, weave, and E. withe. The spelling with f is due to confusion with L. ferrum iron.

ferry.etymology: OE. ferien to convey, AS. ferian, from faran to go; akin to Icel. ferja to ferry, Goth. farjan to sail. See Fare.

fertile.etymology: L. fertilis, fr. ferr to bear, produce: cf. F. fertile. See Bear to support.

ferule.etymology: L. ferula: cf. F. férule. See Ferula.

fervent.etymology: F. fervent, L. fervens, -entis. p.pr. of fervere o the boiling hot, to boil, glow.

fervid.etymology: L. fervidus, fr. fervere. See Fervent.

fervor.etymology: OF. fervor, fervour, F. ferveur, L. fervor, fr. fervere. See Fervent.

fescue.etymology: OE. festu, OF. festu, F. fétu, fr. L. festuca stalk, straw.

fess.etymology: OF. fesse, faisse, F. fasce, fr. L. fascia band. See Fascia.

fesse.etymology: OF. fesse, faisse, F. fasce, fr. L. fascia band. See Fascia.

festal.etymology: L. festum holiday, feast. See feast.

fester.etymology: OE. festern, fr. fester, n.; or fr. OF. festrir, fr. festre, n. See Fester, n.

festinate.etymology: L. festinatus, p.p. of festinare to hasten.

festival.etymology: OF. festival, fr. L. festivum festive jollity, fr. festivus festive, gay. See Festive.

festive.etymology: L. festivus, fr. festum holiday, feast. See feast, and cf. Festivous.

festoon.etymology: F. feston (cf. Sp. feston, It. festone), prob. fr. L. festum festival. See Feast.

fet.etymology: Cf. feat, F. fait, and It. fett slice, G. fetzen rag, Icel. fat garment.

fetch.etymology: OE. fecchen, AS. feccan, perh. the same word as fetian; or cf. facian to wish to get, OFries. faka to prepare. sq. root 77. Cf. Fet, v. t.

fetich.etymology: F. fétiche, from Pg. feiti, adj., n., sorcery, charm, fr. L. facticius made by art, artifical, factitious. See Factitious.

fetid.etymology: L. fetidus, foetidus, fr. fetere, foetere, to have an ill smell, to stink: cf. F. fétide.

fetish.etymology: F. fétiche, from Pg. feiti, adj., n., sorcery, charm, fr. L. facticius made by art, artifical, factitious. See Factitious.

fetlock.etymology: OE. fetlak, fitlock, cf. Icel. fet pace, step, fit webbed foot of water birds, akin to E. foot. sq. root 77. See Foot.

fetter.etymology: AS. fetor, feter; akin to OS. feter, pl., OD. veter, OHG. fezzera, Icel. fjöturr, L. pedi, Gr. foot. sq. root 77. See Foot.

fettle.etymology: OE. & Prov. E., to fettle (in sense 1), fettle, n., order, repair, preparation, dress; prob. akin to E. fit. See Fit, a.

fetus.etymology: L. fetus, foetus, a bringing forth, brood, offspring, young ones, cf. fetus fruitful, fructified, that is or was filled with young; akin to E. fawn a deer, fecundity, felicity, feminine, female, and prob. to do, or according to others, to be.

feud.etymology: OE. feide, AS. f, fr. fah hostile; akin to OHG. f, G. fehde, Sw. fejd, D. feide; prob. akin to E. fiend. See Foe.

fever.etymology: OE. fever, fefer, AS. fefer, fefor, L. febris: cf. F. fièvre. Cf. Febrile.

feverfew.etymology: AS. feferfuge, fr. L. febrifugia. See fever, Fugitive, and cf. Febrifuge.

few.etymology: OE. fewe, feawe, AS. feá, pl. feáwe; akin to OS. fah, OHG. f*, Icel. far, Sw. få, pl., Dan. faa, pl., Goth. faus, L. paucus, cf. Gr. Paucity.

fey.etymology: AS. f, Icel. feigr, OHG. feigi.

fez.etymology: F., fr. the town of Fez in Morocco.

fiat.etymology: L., let it be done, 3d pers. sing., subj. pres., fr. fieri, used as pass. of facere to make. Cf. Be.

fib.etymology: Prob. fr. fable; cf. Prov. E. fibble-fabble nonsense.

fibril.etymology: F. fibrille, dim. of fibre, L. fibra.

fibrocartilage.etymology: L. fibra a fiber + E. cartilage.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.
A suffix used in medical terms to denote a morbid condition of some part, usually some kind of tumor; as in fibroma, glaucoma.

fickle.etymology: OE. fikel untrustworthy, deceitful, AS. ficol, fr. fic, gefic, fraud, deceit; cf. facen deceit, OS. f, OHG. feichan, Icel. feikn portent. Cf. Fidget.

fiction.etymology: F. fiction, L. fictio, fr. fingere, fictum to form, shape, invent, feign. See Feign.

fiddle.etymology: OE. fidele, fithele, AS. fi; akin to D. vedel, OHG. fidula, G. fiedel, Icel. fi, and perh. to E. viol. Cf. Viol.

fidelity.etymology: L. fidelitas: cf. F. fidélité. See Fealty.

fidget.etymology: From Fidge; cf. OE. fiken to fidget, to flatter, Icel. fika to hasten, Sw. fika to hunt after, AS. befician to deceive. Cf. Fickle.

fiducial.etymology: L. fiducia trust, confidence; akin to fides faith. See Faith.

fiduciary.etymology: L. fiduciarus, fr. fiducia: cf. F. fiduciaire. See Fiducial.

fief.etymology: F. fief; of German origin, and the same word as E. fee. See Fee, and cf. Feud, a tief.

field.etymology: OE. feld, fild, AS. feld; akin to D. veld, G. feld, Sw. fält, Dan. felt, Icel. fold field of grass, AS. folde earth, land, ground, OS. folda.

fieldfare.etymology: OE. feldfare, AS. feldfare; field + faran to travel.

fiend.etymology: OE. fend, find, fiend, feond, fiend, foe, AS. feónd; akin to OS. fiond, D. vijand enemy, OHG. fiant, G. feind, Icel. fjand, Sw. & Dan. fiende, Goth. fijands; orig. p.pr. of a verb meaning to hate, AS. feón, feógan, OHG. fi, Goth. fijan, Skr. piy to scorn; prob. akin to E. feud a quarrel. *81. Cf. Foe, Friend.

fierce.etymology: OE. fers, fiers, OF. fier, nom. fiers, fierce, savage, cruel, F. fier proud, from L. ferus wild, savage, cruel; perh. akin to E. bear the animal. Cf. Feral, Ferocity.

fife.etymology: F. fifre, OHG. pfifa, LL. pipa pipe, pipare to play on the pipe, fr. L. pipire, pipare, to peep, pip, chirp, as a chiken. See Pipe.

fifteen.etymology: OE. fiftene, AS. fift, fift. See Five, and Ten, and cf. Fifty.

fifteenth.etymology: OE. fiftenthe; cf. fiftethe, AS. fifte. See Fifteen.

fifth.etymology: OE. fifte, fifthe, AS. fifta. See Five.

fifty.etymology: AS. fiftig; akin to OHG. finfzug, fimfzug, G. fünfzig, funfzig, Goth. fimftigjus. See Five, and Ten, and cf. Fifteen.

fig.etymology: F. figue the fruit of the tree, Pr. figa, fr. L. ficus fig tree, fig. Cf. Fico.

fight.etymology: OE. fihten, fehten, AS. feohtan; akin to D. vechten, OHG. fehtan, G. fechten, Sw. fäkta, Dan. fegte, and perh. to E. fist; cf. L. pugnare to fight, pugnus fist.

figment.etymology: L. figmentum, fr. fingere to form, shape, invent, feign. See Feign.

figurative.etymology: L. figurativus: cf. F. figuratif. See Figurative.

figure.etymology: F., figure, L. figura; akin to fingere to form, shape, feign. See Feign.

filament.etymology: F. filament, fr. L. filum thread. See File a row.

filaria.etymology: NL., fr. L. filum a thread.

filature.etymology: LL. filatura, fr. filare to spin: cf. F. filature. See Filatory.

filbert.etymology: Perh. fr. fill + bread, as filling the bread or husk; cf. G. bartnuss (lit., bread nut) filbert; or perh. named from a St.Philibert, whose day, Aug. 22, fell in the nutting season.

filch.etymology: Cf. AS. feol to stick to, OHG. felhan, felahan, to hide, Icel. fela, Goth. filhan to hide, bury, Prov. E. feal to hide slyly, OE. felen.

file.etymology: F. file row (cf. Pr., Sp., Pg., & It. fila), LL. fila, fr. L. filum a thread. Cf. Enfilade, Filament, Fillet.

filial.etymology: L. filialis, fr. filius son, filia daughter; akin to e. female, feminine. Cf. Fitz.

filiation.etymology: LL. filiatio, fr. L. filius son: cf. F. filiation. See Filial.

filibuster.etymology: Sp. flibuster, flibustero, corrupted fr. E. freebooter. See Freebooter.

filicide.etymology: L. filius son, filia daughter + caedere to kill.

filiform.etymology: L. filum thread + -form: cf. F. filiforme.

fillet.etymology: OE. filet, felet, fr. OF. filet thread, fillet of meat, dim. of fil a thread, fr. L. filum. See Fille a row.

filly.etymology: Cf. Icel. fylia, fr. foli foal. See Foal.

film.etymology: AS. film skin, fr. fell skin; akin to fylmen membrane, OFries. filmene skin. See Fell skin.

fils.etymology: F., fr. L. filius. See Filial.

filter.etymology: F. filtre, the same word as feutre felt, LL. filtrum, feltrum, felt, fulled wool, this being used for straining liquors. See Feuter.

filth.etymology: OE. filthe, fulthe, AS. f, fr. ful foul; akin to OHG. fulida. See Foul, and cf. File.

fimbriate.etymology: L. fimbriatus fibrous, fringed, fr. fimbria fiber, fringe. See Fringe.

final.etymology: F., fr. L. finalis, fr. finis boundary, limit, end. See Finish.

finance.etymology: F., fr. LL. financia payment of money, money, fr. finare to pay a fine or subsidy (cf. OF. finer to finish, pay), fr. L. finis end. See Fine, n., Finish.

finch.etymology: AS. finc; akin to D. vink, OHG. fincho, G. fink; cf. W. pinc a finch; also E. spink.

find.etymology: AS. findan; akin to D. vinden, OS. & OHG. findan, G. finden, Dan. finde, icel. & Sw. finna, Goth. fin; and perh. to L. petere to seek, Gr. pat to fall, fly, E. petition.

fine.etymology: F. fin, LL. finus fine, pure, fr. L. finire to finish; cf. finitus, p.p., finished, completed (hence the sense accomplished, perfect.) See Finish, and cf. Finite.

finesse.etymology: F., fr. fin fine. See Fine, a.

finger.etymology: AS. finger; akin to D. vinger, OS. & OHG. fingar, G. finger, Icel. fingr, Sw. & Dan. finger, Goth. figgrs; of unknown origin; perh. akin to E. fang.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix, commonly having a diminutive or a depreciatory force; as in duck-ling, dosling, hireling, fosterling, firstling, underling.

finial.etymology: L. finire to finish, end. See Finish.

finish.etymology: F. finir (with a stem finiss- in several forms, whence E. - ish: see -ish.),fr. L. finire to limit, finish, end, fr. finis boundary, limit, end; perh. for fidnis, and akin findere to cleave, E. fissure.

finite.etymology: L. finitus, p.p. of finire. See Finish, and cf. Fine, a.

fipple.etymology: perh. fr. L. fibula a clasp, a pin; cf. Prov. E. fible a stick used to stir pottage.

fire.etymology: OE. fir, fyr, fur AS. fr; akin to D. vuur, OS. & OHG. fiur, G. feuer, Icel. f, f, Gr. purus pure, E. pure Cf. Empyrean, Pyre.

firedrake.etymology: AS. f; f fire + draca a dragon. See Fire, and Drake a dragon.

firestone.etymology: AS. f flint; f fire + stan stone.

firkin.etymology: From AS. feówer four (or an allied word, perh. Dutch or Danish) + -kin. See Four.

roots.meaning: A diminutive suffix; as, manikin; lambkin.

firm.etymology: OE. ferme, F. ferme, fr.L. firmus; cf. Skr. dharman support, law, order, dh to hold fast, carry. Cf. Farm, Throne.

firmament.etymology: L. firmamentum, fr. firmare to make firm: cf. F. firmament. See Firm, v. & a.

first.etymology: OE. first, furst, AS. fyrst; akin to Icel. fyrstr, Sw. & Dan. förste, OHG. furist, G. fürst prince; a superlatiye form of E. for, fore. See For, Fore, and cf. Formeer, Foremost.

fisc.etymology: F. fisc, fr. L. fiscus basket, money basket, treasury; prob. akin to fascis bundle. See Fasces.

fiscal.etymology: F. fiscal, L. fiscalis, fr. fiscus. See Fisc.

fish.etymology: F. fiche peg, mark, fr. fisher to fix.

fissile.etymology: L. fissilis, fr. fissus, p.p. of findere to split. See Fissure.

fissiparous.etymology: L. fissus (p.p. of findere to split) + parere to bring forth: cf. F. fissipare.

fissipedia.etymology: NL., fr. L. fissus (p.p. of findere to cleave) + pes, pedis, a foot.

fissure.etymology: L. fissura, fr. findere, fissum, to cleave, split; akin to E. bite: cf. F. fissure.

fissurella.etymology: NL., dim. of L. fissura a fissure.

fist.etymology: OE. fist, fust, AS. f; akin to D. vuist, OHG. f, G. faust, and prob. to L. pugnus, Gr. Pugnacious, Pigmy.

fistulate.etymology: Cf. L. fistulatus furnished with pipes.

five.etymology: OE. fif, five, AS. fif, fife; akin to D. vijf, OS. fif, OHG. finf, funf, G. fünf, Icel. fimm, Sw. & Sw. Dan. fem, Goth. fimf, Lith. penki, W. pump, OIr. cóic, L. quinque, Gr. pa. Fifth, Cinque, Pentagon, Punch the drink, Quinary.

fix.etymology: OE., fr. L. fixus, p.p. of figere to fix; cf. F. fixe.

fizz.etymology: Cf. Icel. fisa to break wind, Dan. fise to foist, fizzle, OSw. fisa, G. fisten, feisten. Cf. Foist.

flaccid.etymology: L. flaccidus, fr. flaccus flabby: cf. OF. flaccide.

flag.etymology: Cf. Icel. flaka to droop, hang loosely. Cf. Flacker, Flag an ensign.

flagellant.etymology: L. flagellans, p.p. of flagellare: cf.F. flagellant. See Flagellate.

flagellata.etymology: NL., fr.L. flagellatus, p. p. See Flagellate, v. t.

flagellate.etymology: L. flagellatus, p.p. of flagellare to scoure, fr. flagellum whip, dim. of flagrum whip, scoure; cf. fligere to strike. Cf. Flall.

flagellum.etymology: L., a whip. See Flagellate, v. t.

flageolet.etymology: F. flageolet, dim. of OF. flaj (as if fr. a LL. flautio;us), of flaüte, flahute, F. fl. See Flute.

flagitious.etymology: L. flagitiosus, fr. flagitium a shameful or disgraceful act, orig., a burning desire, heat of passion, from flagitare to demand hotly, fiercely; cf. flagrare to burn, E. flagrant.

flagon.etymology: F. flacon, for flascon, fr. OF. flasche, from LL. flasco. See Flask.

flagrant.etymology: L. flagrans, -antis, p.pr. of flagrate to burn, akin to Gr. flagrant. Cf. Flame, Phlox.

flail.etymology: L. flagellum whip, scourge, in LL., a threshing flail: cf. OF. flael, flaiel, F. fléau. See Flagellum.

flair.etymology: OE. flaireodor, fr. OF. & F. flair, fr. OF. flairier, F. flairer, to smell, LL. flagrare for L. fragrare. See Flagrant.

flake.etymology: Cf. Icel. flaki, fleki, Dan. flage, D. vlaak.

flambe.etymology: F., p.p. of flamber to singe, pass (a thing) through flame. Cf. Flambeau.

flambeau.etymology: F., fr. OF. flambe flame, for flamble, from L. flammula a little flame, dim. of flamma flame. See Flame.

flame.etymology: OE. flame, flaume, flaumbe, OF. flame, flambe, F. flamme, fr. L. flamma, fr. flamma, fr. flagrare to burn. See Flagrant, and cf. Flamneau, Flamingo.

flamingo.etymology: Sp. flamenco, cf. Pg. flamingo, Prov. flammant, F. flamant; prop. a p.pr. meaning flaming. So called in allusion to its color. See Flame.

flange.etymology: Prov. E. flange to project, flanch a projection. See Flanch, Flank.

flank.etymology: F. flanc, prob. fr. L. flaccus flabby, with n inserted. Cf. Flaccid, Flanch, Flange.

flannel.etymology: F. flanelle, cf. OF. flaine a pillowcase, a mattress; fr. W. gwlanen flannel, fr. gwlan wool; prob. akin to E. wool. Cf. Wool.

flap.etymology: OE. flappe, flap, blow, bly-flap; cf. D. flap, and E. flap, v.

flare.etymology: Cf. Norw. flara to blaze, flame, adorn with tinsel, dial. Sw. flasa upp, and E. flash, or flacker.

flash.etymology: Cf. OE. flaskien, vlaskien to pour, sprinkle, dial. Sw. flasa to blaze, E. flush, flare.

flask.etymology: AS. flasce, flaxe; akin to D. flesch, OHG. flasca, G. flasche, Icel. & Sw. flaska, Dan. flaske, OF. flasche, LL. flasca, flasco; of uncertain origin; cf. L. vasculum, dim. of vas a vessel, Gr. Flagon, Flasket.

flat.etymology: Akin to Icel. flatr, Sw. flat, Dan. flad, OHG. flaz, and AS. flet floor, G. flötz stratum, layer.

flatter.etymology: OE. flateren, cf. OD. flatteren; akin to G. flattern to flutter, Icel. fla to fawn, flatter: cf. F. flatter. Cf. Flitter, Flutter, Flattery.

flattery.etymology: OE. flaterie, OF. flaterie, F. flaterie, fr. flater to flatter, F. flatter; of uncertain origin. See Flatter, v. t.

flatulent.etymology: L. flatus a blowing, flatus ventris windiness, flatulence, fr. flare to blow: cf. F. flatulent. See Blow.

flaunt.etymology: Cf. dial. G. flandern to flutter, wave; perh. akin to E. flatter, flutter.

flautist.etymology: It. flauto a flute See Flute.

flavor.etymology: OF. fleur, flaur (two syllables), odor, cf. F. fleurer to emit an odor, It. flatore a bad odor, prob. fr. L. flare to bow, whence the sense of exhalation. Cf. Blow.

flaw.etymology: OE. flai, flaw flake; cf. Sw. flaga flaw, crack, breach, flake, D. vlaag gust of wind, Norw. flage, flaag, and E. flag a flat stone.

flax.etymology: AS. fleax; akin to D. vlas, OHG. flahs, G. flachs, and prob. to flechten to braid, plait,m twist, L. plectere to weave, plicare to fold, Gr. Ply.

flay.etymology: OE. flean, flan, AS. fleán; akin to D. vlaen, Icel. fla, Sw. flå, Dan. flaae, cf. Lith. ples to tear, plyszti, v.i., to burst tear; perh. akin to E. flag to flat stone, flaw.

fleck.etymology: Cf. Icel. flekkr; akin to Sw. fläck, D. vlek, G. fleck, and perh. to E. flitch.

fledge.etymology: OE. flegge, flygge; akin to D. vlug, G. flügge, flücke, OHG. flucchi, Icel. fleygr, and to E. fly. Fly, v. i.

flee.etymology: OE. fleon, fleen, AS. fleón (imperf. fleáh); akin to D. vlieden, OHG. & OS. fliohan, G. fliehen, Icel. fl (imperf. fl), Dan. flye, Sw. fly (imperf. flydde), Goth. pliuhan. (Flight.

fleece.etymology: OE. flees, AS. fleós; akin to D. flies, vlies .

fleer.etymology: OE. flerien; cf. Scot. fleyr, Norw. flira to titter, giggle, laugh at nothing, MHG. vlerre, vlarre, a wide wound.

fleet.etymology: OE. fleten, fleoten, to swim, AS. fleótan to swim, float; akin to D. vlieten to flow, OS. fliotan, OHG. fliozzan, G. fliessen, Icel. fljota to float, flow, Sw. flyta, D. flyde, L. pluere to rain, Gr. plu to swim, sail. sq. root84. Cf. Fleet, n. & a., Float, Pluvial, Flow.

flense.etymology: Cf. Dan. flense, D. vlensen, vlenzen, Scot. flinch.

flesh.etymology: OE. flesch, flesc, AS. fl; akin to OFries. flask, D. vleesch, OS. fl, OHG. fleisc, G. fleisch, Icel. & Dan. flesk lard, bacon, pork, Sw. fläsk.

flex.etymology: L. flexus, p.p. of flectere to bend, perh. flectere and akin to falx sickle, E. falchion. Cf. Flinch.

flexuous.etymology: L. flexuosus, fr. flexus a bending, turning.

flicker.etymology: OE. flikeren, flekeren, to flutter, AS. flicerian, flicorian, cf. D. flikkeren to sparkle. Flacker.

flight.etymology: AS. fliht, flyht, a flying, fr. fleógan to fly; cf. flyht a fleeing, fr. fleón to flee, G. flucht a fleeing, Sw. flykt, G. flug a flying, Sw. flygt, D. vlugt a fleeing or flying, Dan. flugt. sq. root84. See Flee, Fly.

flimsy.etymology: Cf. W. llumsi naked, bare, empty, slouggish, spiritless. Cf. Limsy.

flinch.etymology: Prob. fr. OE. flecchen to waver, give way, F. fléchir, fr. L. flectere to bend; but prob. influenced by E. blench. Cf. Flex.

flinders.etymology: Scot. flenders, flendris; perh. akin to E. flutter; cf. D. flenters rags, broken pieces.

fling.etymology: OE. flingen, flengen, to rush, hurl; cf. Icel. flengia to whip, ride furiously, OSw. flenga to strike, Sw. flänga to romp, Dan. flenge to slash.

flint.etymology: AS. flint, akin to Sw. flinta, Dan. flint; cf. OHG. flins flint, G. flinte gun (cf. E. flintlock), perh. akin to Gr. Plinth.

flip.etymology: Cf. Prov. E. flip nimble, flippant, also, a slight blow. Cf. Flippant.

flippant.etymology: Prov. E. flip to move nimbly; cf. W. llipa soft, limber, pliant, or Icel. fleipa to babble, prattle. Cf. Flip, Fillip, Flap, Flipper.

flirt.etymology: Cf. AS. fleard trifle, folly, fleardian to trifle.

flit.etymology: OE. flitten, flutten, to carry away; cf. Icel. flytja, Sw. flytta, Dan. flytte. Fleet, v. i.

flitch.etymology: OE. flicche, flikke, AS. flicce, akin to Icel. flikki; cf. Icel. flik flap, tatter; perh. akin to E. fleck. Cf. Flick, n.

flitter.etymology: Cf. G. flitter spangle, tinsel, flittern to make a tremulous motion, to glitter. Cf. Flitter, v. i.

float.etymology: OE. flote ship, boat, fleet, AS. flota ship, fr. fleótan to float; akin to D. vloot fleet, G. floss raft, Icel. floti float, raft, fleet, Sw. flotta. sq. root 84. See Fleet, v. i., and cf. Flotilla, Flotsam, Plover.

flock.etymology: AS. flocc flock, company; akin to Icel. flokkr crowd, Sw. flock, Dan. flok; prob. orig. used of flows, and akin to E. fly. See Fly.

floe.etymology: Cf. Dan. flag af iis, iisflage, Sw. flaga, flake, isflaga, isflake. See Flag a flat stone.

flog.etymology: Cf. Scot. fleg blow, stroke, kick, AS. flocan to strike, or perh. fr. L. flagellare to whip. Cf. Flagellate.

flood.etymology: OE. flod a flowing, stream, flood, AS. flod; akin to D. vloed, OS. flod, OHG. fluot, G. flut, Icel. floedh, Sw. & Dan. flod, Goth. flodus; from the root of E. flow. sq. root80. See Flow, v. i.

floor.etymology: AS. fl; akin to D. vloer, G. flur field, floor, entrance hall, Icel. fl floor of a cow stall, cf. Ir. & Gael. lar floor, ground, earth, W. llawr, perh. akin to L. planus level. Cf. Plain smooth.

flora.etymology: L., the goddess of flowers, from flos, floris, flower. See Flower.

floral.etymology: L. Floralis belonging to Flora: cf. F. floral. See Flora.

floreal.etymology: F. floréal, fr. L. flos, floris, flower.

florence.etymology: From the city of Florence: cf. F. florence a kind of cloth, OF. florin.

florentine.etymology: L. Florentinus, fr. Florentia Florence: cf. F. florentin.

floret.etymology: OF. florete, F. fleurette, dim. of OF. lor, F. fleur. See Flower, and cf. Floweret, 3d Ferret.

floriculture.etymology: L. flos, floris, flower + cultura culture.

florid.etymology: L. floridus, fr. flos, floris, flower. See Flower.

florin.etymology: F. florin, It. florino, orig., a Florentine coin, with a lily on it, fr. flore a flower, fr. L. flos. See Flower, and cf. Floren.

florist.etymology: Cf. F. fleuriste, floriste, fr. F. fleur flower. See Flower.

floss.etymology: It. floscio flabby, soft, fr. L. fluxus flowing, loose, slack. See Flux, n.

flotation.etymology: Cf. F. flottation a floating, flottaison water line, fr. flotter to float. See Flotilla.

flotilla.etymology: Sp. flotilla, dim. of flota fleet; akin to F. flotte, It. flotta, and F. flot wave, fr. L. fluctus, but prob. influenced by words akin to E. float. See Fluctuate, and cf. Float, n.

flotsam.etymology: F. flotter to float. See FFlotilla, and cf. Jetsam.

flounder.etymology: Cf. Sw. flundra; akin to Dan. flynder, Icel. fly, G. flunder, and perh. to E. flounder, v.i.

flour.etymology: F. fleur de farine the flower (i.e., the best) of meal, cf. Sp. flor de la harina superfine flour, Icel. flür flower, flour. See Flower.

flourish.etymology: OE. florisshen, flurisshen, OF. flurir, F. fleurir, fr. L. florere to bloom, fr. flos, floris, flower. See Flower, and -ish.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to from adjectives from nouns and from adjectives. It denotes relation, resemblance, similarity, and sometimes has a diminutive force; as, selfish, boyish, brutish; whitish, somewhat white.

flout.etymology: OD. fluyten to play the flute, to jeer, D. fluiten, fr. fluit, fr. French. See Flute.

flow.etymology: AS. flowan; akin to D. vloeijen, OHG. flawen to wash, Icel. floa to deluge, Gr. float, fleet. *80. Cf. Flood.

flower.etymology: OE. flour, OF. flour, flur, flor, F. fleur, fr. L. flos, floris. Cf. Blossom, Effloresce, Floret, Florid, Florin, Flour, Flourish.

fluctuate.etymology: L. fluctuatus, p.p. of fluctuare, to wave, fr. fluctus wave, fr. fluere, fluctum, to flow. See Fluent, and cf. Flotilla.

flue.etymology: Cf. OF. flue a flowing, fr. fluer to flow, fr. L. fluere (cf. Fluent); a perh. a corruption of E. flute.

fluency.etymology: L. fluentia: cf. F. fluence. See Fluent.

fluent.etymology: L. fluens, -entis, p.pr. of fluere to flow; cf. Gr. Fluctuate, Flux.

fluid.etymology: L. fluidus, fr. fluere to flow: cf. F. fluide. See Fluent.

fluke.etymology: Cf. LG. flunk, flunka wing, the palm of an anchor; perh. akin to E. fly.

flume.etymology: Cf. OE. flum river, OF, flum, fr. L. flumen, fr. fluere to flow. *84. See Fluent.

flummery.etymology: W. llumru, or llumruwd, a kind of food made of oatmeal steeped in water until it has turned sour, fr. llumrig harsh, raw, crude, fr. llum sharp, severe.

flunky.etymology: Prob. fr. or akin to flank.

fluor.etymology: L., a flowing, fr. fluere to flow. See Fluent.

fluorine.etymology: NL. fluorina: cf. G. fluorin, F. fluorine. So called from its occurrence in the mineral fluorite.

roots.meaning: A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.

flush.etymology: Cf. OE. fluschen to fly up, penetrate, F. fluz a flowing, E. flux, dial. Sw. flossa to blaze, and E. flash; perh. influenced by blush. *84.

fluster.etymology: Cf. Icel. flaustra to be flustered, flaustr a fluster.

flute.etymology: OE. floute, floite, fr. OF. flaüte, flahute, flahuste, F. fl; cf. LL. flauta, D. fluit. See Flute, v. i.

fluvial.etymology: L. fluvialis, from fluvius river, fr. fluere to flow: cf.F. fluvial. See Fluent.

flux.etymology: L. fluxus, fr. fluere, fluxum,to flow: cf.F. flux. See Fluent, and cf. 1st & 2d Floss, Flush, n., 6.

fly.etymology: OE. fleen, fleen, fleyen, flegen, AS. fleógan; akin to D. vliegen, ONG. fliogan, G. fliegen, Icel. flj, Sw. flyga, Dan. flyve, Goth. us- flaugjan to cause to fly away, blow about, and perh. to L. pluma feather, E. plume. Fledge, Flight, Flock of animals.

foal.etymology: OE. fole, AS. fola; akin to OHG. folo, G. fohlen, Goth. fula, Icel. foli, Sw Lfle, Gr., L. pullus a young animal. Cf. Filly, Poultry, Pullet.

foam.etymology: OE. fam, fom, AS. fm; akin to OHG. & G. feim.

focus.etymology: L. focus hearth, fireplace; perh. akin to E. bake. Cf. Curfew, Fuel, Fusil the firearm.

foe.etymology: OE. fo, fa, AS. fh hostile; prob. akin to E. fiend. sq. root81.

fog.etymology: Cf. Scot. fog, fouge, moss, foggag rank grass, LL. fogagium, W. ffug dry grass.

foil.etymology: F. fouler to tread or trample under one's feet, to press, oppress. See Full, v. t.

foist.etymology: OF. fuste stick, boat, fr. L. fustis cudgel. Cf. 1st Fust.

fold.etymology: OE. folden, falden, AS. fealdan; akin to OHG. faltan, faldan, G. falten, Icel. falda, Dan. folde, Sw. fålla, Goth. fal, cf. Gr.pu a fold. Cf. Fauteuil.

foliage.etymology: OF. foillage, fueillage, F. feuillage, fr. OF. foille, fueille, fueil, F. feulle, leaf, L. folium. See 3d Foil, and cf. Foliation, Filemot.

foliate.etymology: L. foliatus leaved, leafy, fr. folium leaf. See Foliage.

folio.etymology: Ablative of L. folium leaf. See 4th Foil.

folk.etymology: AS. folc; akin to D. volk, OS. & OHG. folk, G. volk, Icel. f, Sw. & Dan. folk, Lith. pulkas crowd, and perh. to E. follow.

folks.etymology: AS. folc; akin to D. volk, OS. & OHG. folk, G. volk, Icel. f, Sw. & Dan. folk, Lith. pulkas crowd, and perh. to E. follow.

follicle.etymology: L. folliculus a small bag, husk, pod, dim of follis bellows, an inflated ball, a leathern money bag, perh. akin to E. bellows: cf. F. follicule. Cf. 2d Fool.

follow.etymology: OE. foluwen, folwen, folgen, AS. folgian, fylgean, fylgan; akin to D. volgen, OHG. folg, G. folgen, Icel. fylgja, Sw. följa, Dan. fölge, and perh. to E. folk.

folly.etymology: OE. folie, foli, F. folie, fr. fol, fou, foolish, mad. See Fool.

foment.etymology: F. fomenter, fr. L. fomentare, fr. fomentum (for fovimentum) a warm application or lotion, fr. fovere to warm or keep warm; perh. akin to Gr. bake.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

fond.etymology: For fonned, p. p. of OE. fonnen to be foolish. See Fon.

fondant.etymology: F., lit., melting, p. pr. of fondre to melt, L. fundere. See Found to cast.

fondu.etymology: F. fondu, p.p. of fondre to melt, blend. See Found to cast.

font.etymology: F. fonte, fr. fondre to melt or cast. See Found to cast, and cf. Fount a font.

fontanel.etymology: F. fontanelle, prop., a little fountain, fr. fontaine fountain. See Fountain.

food.etymology: OE. fode, AS. foda; akin to Icel. fæ\'eba, fæ\'ebi, Sw. föda, Dan. & LG. föde, OHG. fatunga, Gr. patei^sthai to eat, and perh. to Skr. pa to protect, L. pascere to feed, pasture, pabulum food, E. pasture. *75. Cf. Feed, Fodder food, Foster to cherish.

fool.etymology: Cf. F. fouler to tread, crush. Cf. 1st Foil.

foolhardy.etymology: OF. folhardi. See Fool idiot, and Hardy.

foolscap.etymology: So called from the watermark of a fool's cap and bells used by old paper makers. See Fool's cap, under Fool.

foot.etymology: OE. fot, foot, pl. feet. AS. f, pl. f; akin to D. voet, OHG. fuoz, G. fuss, Icel. f, Sw. fot, Dan. fod, Goth. f, L. pes, Gr. pad, Icel. fet step, pace measure of a foot, feta to step, find one's way. *77, 250. Cf. Antipodes, Cap-a-pie, Expedient, Fet to fetch, Fetlock, Fetter, Pawn a piece in chess, Pedal.

fop.etymology: OE. foppe, fop, fool; cf. E. fob to cheat, G. foppen to make a fool of one, jeer, D. foppen.

forage.etymology: OF. fourage, F. fourrage, fr. forre, fuerre, fodder, straw, F. feurre, fr. LL. foderum, fodrum, of German or Scand, origin; cf. OHG. fuotar, G. futter. See Fodder food, and cf. Foray.

foramen.etymology: L., fr. forare to bore, pierce.

foraminifera.etymology: NL., fr. L. foramen, -aminis, a foramen + ferre to bear.

foray.etymology: Another form of forahe. Cf. Forray.

forbear.etymology: See Fore, and Bear to produce.

forbid.etymology: OE. forbeden, AS. forbeódan; pref. for- + beódan to bid; akin to D. verbieden, G. verbieten, Icel., fyrirbjoedha, forboedha, Sw. förbjuda, Dan. forbyde. See Bid, v. t.

roots.meaning: A prefix to verbs, having usually the force of a negative or privative. It often implies also loss, detriment, or destruction, and sometimes it is intensive, meaning utterly, quite thoroughly, as in forbathe.

forcemeat.etymology: Corrupt. for farce-meat, fr. F. farce stuffing. See Farce, n.

forceps.etymology: L. forceps, -cipis, from the root of formus Hot + capere to take; akin to E. heave. Cf. Furnace.

forcible.etymology: Cf. OF. forcible forcible, forceable that may be forced.

ford.etymology: AS. ford; akin to G. furt, Icel. f bay, and to E. fare. Fare, v. i., and cf. Frith arm of the sea.

fore.etymology: AS. f, fr. faran to go. See Fare, v. i.

forebode.etymology: AS. forebodian; fore + bodian to announce. See Bode v. t.

foreclose.etymology: F. forclos, p.p. of forclore to exclude; OF. fors, F. hors, except, outside (fr. L. foris outside) + F. clore to close. See Foreign, and Close, v. t.

forefend.etymology: OE. forfenden; pref. for- + fenden to fend. See Fend, v. t.

roots.meaning: A prefix to verbs, having usually the force of a negative or privative. It often implies also loss, detriment, or destruction, and sometimes it is intensive, meaning utterly, quite thoroughly, as in forbathe.

foreign.etymology: OE. forein, F. forain, LL. foraneus, fr. L. foras, foris, out of doors, abroad, without; akin to fores doors, and E. door. See Door, and cf. Foreclose, Forfeit, Forest, Forum.

foremost.etymology: OE. formest first, AS. formest, fyrmest, superl. of forma first, which is a superl. fr. fore fore; cf. Goth. frumist, fruma, first. See Fore, adv., and cf. First, Former, Frame, v. t., Prime, a.

forensic.etymology: L. forensis, fr. forum a public place, market place. See Forum.

foresee.etymology: AS. foreseón; fore + seón to see. See See, v. t.

foreshow.etymology: AS. foresceáwian to foresee, provide; fore + sceáwian to see. See Show, v. t.

forest.etymology: OF. forest, F. forêt, LL. forestis, also, forestus, forestum, foresta, prop., open ground reserved for the chase, fr. L. foris, foras, out of doors, abroad. See Foreign.

forestall.etymology: OE. forstallen to stop, to obstruct; to stop (goods) on the way to the market by buying them beforehand, from forstal obstruction, AS. forsteal, foresteall, prop., a placing one's self before another. See Fore, and Stall.

forfeit.etymology: OE. forfet crime, penalty, F. forfait crime (LL. forefactum, forifactum), prop. p.p. of forfaire to forfeit, transgress, fr. LL. forifacere, prop., to act beyond; L. foris out of doors, abroad, beyond + facere to do. See Foreign, and FAct.

forficula.etymology: L., small shears, scissors, dim. of forfex shears.

forge.etymology: F. forge, fr. L. fabrica the workshop of an artisan who works in hard materials, fr. faber artisan, smith, as adj., skillful, ingenious; cf. Gr. Fabric.

forger.etymology: Cf. F. forgeur metal worker, L. fabricator artificer. See Forge, n. & v. t., and cf. Fabricator.

forget.etymology: OE. forgeten, foryeten, AS. forgietan, forgitan; pref. for- + gietan, gitan (only in comp.), to get; cf. D. vergeten, G. vergessen, Sw. förgäta, Dan. forgiette. See For-, and Get, v. t.

forgive.etymology: OE. forgiven, foryiven, foryeven, AS. forgiefan, forgifan; perh. for- + giefan, gifan to give; cf. D. vergeven, G. vergeben, Icel. fyrirgefa, Sw. f, Goth. fragiban to give, grant. See For-, and Give, v. t.

forgo.etymology: OE. forgan, forgon, forgoon, AS. forgan, prop., to go past, hence, to abstain from; pref. for- + gan to go; akin to G. vergehen to pass away, to transgress. See Go, v. i.

fork.etymology: AS. forc, fr. L. furca. Cf. Fourch, Furcate.

forlorn.etymology: OE., p.p. of forlesen to lose utterly, AS. forleósan (p.p. forloren); pref. for- + leósan (in comp.) to lose; cf. D. verliezen to lose, G. verlieren, Sw. förlora, Dan. forloren, Goth. fraliusan to lose. See For-, and Lorn, a., Lose, v. t.

former.etymology: A compar. due to OE. formest. See Foremost.

formic.etymology: L. formica an ant: cf. F. formique.

formicary.etymology: LL. formicarium, fr. L. formica an ant.

formication.etymology: L. formicatio, fr. formicare to creep like an ant, to feel as if ants were crawling on one's self, fr. formica ant: cf. F. formication.

formidable.etymology: L. formidabilis, fr. formidare to fear, dread: cf. F. formidable.

formula.etymology: L., dim. of forma form, model. SeeForm, n.

fornicate.etymology: L. fornicatus, fr. fornix, - icis, an arch, vault.

fornicator.etymology: F. fornicateur, OF. fornicator, from L. fornicator.

forsake.etymology: AS. forsacan to oppose, refuse; for- + sacan to contend, strive; akin to Goth. sakan. See For-, and Sake.

forsooth.etymology: AS. forso\'eb; for, prep. + so\'eb sooth, truth. See For, prep., and Sooth.

forswear.etymology: OE. forsweren, forswerien, AS. forswerian; pref. for- + swerian to swear. See For-, and Swear, v. i.

forsythia.etymology: NL. Named after William Forsyth, who brought in from China.

fort.etymology: F., from fort strong, L. fortis; perh. akin to Skr. darh to fix, make firm, and to E. firm Cf. Forte, Force, Fortalice, Comfort, Effort.

forte.etymology: IT. forte: cf. F. fort. See Fort.

forth.etymology: AS. foredh, fr. for akin to D. voort, G. fort sq. root78. See Fore, For, and cf. Afford, Further, adv.

fortify.etymology: F. fortifier, L. fortificare; fortis strong + - ficare (in comp.) to make. See Fort, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

fortissimo.etymology: It., superl. of forte, adv. See Forte, adv.

fortitude.etymology: L. fortitudo, fr. fortis strong. See Fort.

fortnight.etymology: Contr. fr. fourteen nights, our ancestors reckoning time by nights and winters; so, also, seven nights, sennight, a week.

fortress.etymology: F. forteresse, OF. forteresce, fortelesce, LL. foralitia, fr. L. fortis strong. See Fort, and cf. Fortalice.

fortuitous.etymology: L. fortuitus; akin to forte, adv., by chance, prop. abl. of fors, fortis, chance. See Fortune.

fortunate.etymology: L. fortunatus, p.p. of fortunare to make fortunate or prosperous, fr. fortuna. See Fortune, n.

fortune.etymology: F. fortune, L. fortuna; akin to fors, fortis, chance, prob. fr. ferre to bear, bring. See Bear to support, and cf. Fortuitous.

forty.etymology: OE. forti, fourti, fowerty, AS. feówertig; feówer four + suff. -tig ten; akin to OS. fiwartig, fiartig, D. veertig, G. vierzig, Icel. fjörutiu, Sw. fyratio, Dan. fyrretyve, Goth. fidw. See Four, and Ten, and cf. Fourteen.

forum.etymology: L.; akin to foris, foras, out of doors. See Foreign.

forward.etymology: OE., fr. AS. foreweard; fore before + weard a ward. See Ward, n.

forwards.etymology: AS. forweard, foreweard; for, fore + -weardes; akin to G. vorwärts. The s is properly a genitive ending. See For, Fore, and -ward, -wards.

roots.meaning: Suffixes denoting course or direction to; motion or tendency toward; as in backward, or backwards; toward, or towards, etc.

fosse.etymology: F., fr. L. fossa, fr. fodere, fossum, to dig.

fossil.etymology: L. fossilis, fr. fodere to dig: cf. F. fossile. See Fosse.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.

foster.etymology: OE. fostren, fr. AS. foster, fostor, food, nourishment, fr. foda food. *75. See Food.

foumart.etymology: OE. folmard, fulmard; AS. f foul + mear, meard, marten: cf. F. marte, martre. See Foul, a., and Marten the quadruped.

found.etymology: F. fondre, L. fundere to found, pour.

foundation.etymology: F. fondation, L. fundatio. See Found to establish.

founder.etymology: Cf. OF. fondeor, F. fondateur, L. fundator.

foundling.etymology: OE. foundling, fundling; finden to find + - ling; cf. fündling, findling. See Find, v. t., and -ling.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix, commonly having a diminutive or a depreciatory force; as in duck-ling, dosling, hireling, fosterling, firstling, underling.

fountain.etymology: F. fontaine, LL. fontana, fr. L. fons, fontis. See 2d Fount.

four.etymology: OE. four, fower, feower, AS. feówer; akin to OS. fiwar, D. & G. vier, OHG. fior, Icel. fj, Sw. fyra, Dan. fire, Goth. fidw, Russ. chetuire, chetvero, W. pedwar, L. quatuor, Gr. catur. Farthing, Firkin, Forty, Cater four, Quater-cousin, Quatuor, Quire of paper, tetrarch.

fourteen.etymology: OE. fourtene, feowertene, AS. feówert, feówert. See Four, and Ten, and cf. Forty.

fourteenth.etymology: Cf. OE. fourtende, fourtethe, AS. feówerteoedha.

fourth.etymology: OE. fourthe, ferthe, feorthe, AS. feóredha, fr. feówer four.

fox.etymology: AS. fox; akin to D. vos, G. fuchs, OHG. fuhs, foha, Goth. faúh, Icel. f fox, fox fraud; of unknown origin, cf. Skr. puccha tail. Cf. Vixen.

foyer.etymology: F., fr. LL. focarium fireplace. See Focus, n.

fracas.etymology: F., crash, din, tumult, It. fracasso, fr. fracassare to break in pieces, perh. fr. fra within, among (L. infra) + cassare to annul, cashier. Cf. Cashier, v. t.

fraction.etymology: F. fraction, L. fractio a breaking, fr. frangere, fractum, to break. See Break.

fractious.etymology: Cf. Prov. E. frack forward, eager, E. freak, fridge; or Prov. E. fratch to squabble, quarrel.

fracture.etymology: L. fractura, fr. frangere, fractum, to break: cf. F. fracture. See Fraction.

fragile.etymology: L. fragilis, from frangere to break; cf. F. fragile. See Break, v. t., and cf. Frail, a.

fragility.etymology: L. fragilitas: cf. F. fragilité. Cf. Frailty.

fragment.etymology: L. fragmentum, fr. frangere to break: cf. F. fragment. See Break, v. t.

frail.etymology: OE. fraiel, fraile, OF. fraiel, freel, frael, fr. LL. fraellum.

frailty.etymology: OE. frelete, freilte, OF. fraileté, fr. L. fragilitas. See Frail, a., and cf. Fragility.

frame.etymology: OE. framen, fremen, to execute, build, AS. fremman to further, perform, effect, fr. fram strong, valiant; akin to E. foremost, and prob. to AS. fram from, Icel. fremja, frama, to further, framr forward, G. fromm worthy, excellent, pious. See Foremost, From, and cf. Furnish.

franc.etymology: F., fr. franc a Franc. See Frank, a.

franchise.etymology: F., fr. franc, fem. franche, free. See Frank, a.

franciscan.etymology: LL. Franciscus Francis: cf. F. franciscain.

frangipane.etymology: F. frangipane; supposed to be called so from the inventor, the Marquis Frangipani, major general under Louis XIV.

frankincense.etymology: OF. franc free, pure + encens incense.

franklin.etymology: OE. frankelein; cf. LL. franchilanus. See Frank, a.

frantic.etymology: OE. frentik, frenetik, F. frentique, L. phreneticus, from Gr. Frenzy, and cf. Frenetic, Phrenetic.

frap.etymology: Cf. F. frapper to strike, to seize ropes. Cf. Affrap.

frappe.etymology: F., p.p. of frapper to strike, to chill.

fraternal.etymology: F. fraternel, LL. fraternalis, fr. L. fraternus, fr. frater brother. See Brother.

fratricide.etymology: L. fratricidium a brother's murder, fr. fratricida a brother's murderer; frater, fratris, brother + caedere to kill: cf. F. fratricide.

fraud.etymology: F. fraude, L. fraus, fraudis; prob. akin to Skr. dh to injure, dhv to cause to fall, and E. dull.

fraudulent.etymology: L. fraudulentus, fr. fraus, fraudis, frand: cf. F. fraudulent.

fraught.etymology: OE.fraight, fraght; akin to Dan. fragt, Sw. frakt, D. vracht, G. fracht, cf. OHG. fr merit, reward; perh. from corresponding to E. for + The root of E. own. Cf. Freight.

freak.etymology: Akin to OE. frakin, freken, freckle, Icel. freknur, pl., Sw. fräkne, Dan. fregne, Gr. prsçni variegated. Cf. Freckle, Freck.

freckle.etymology: Dim., from the same root as freak, v. t.

free.etymology: OE. fre, freo, AS. freó, fri; akin to D. vrij, OS. & OHG. fri, G. frei, Icel. fri, Sw. & Dan. fri, Goth. freis, and also to Skr. prija beloved, dear, fr. pri to love, Goth. frij. Cf. Affray, Belfry, Friday, Friend, Frith inclosure.

freebooter.etymology: D. vrijbuiter, fr. vrijbuiten to plunder; vrij free + buit booty, akin to E. booty. See Free, and Booty, and cf. Filibuster.

freedom.etymology: AS. freód; freófree + -dom. See Free, and -dom.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting: (a) Jurisdiction or property and jurisdiction, dominion, as in kingdom earldom. (b) State, condition, or quality of being, as in wisdom, freedom.

freeze.etymology: OE. fresen, freosen, AS. freósan; akin to D. vriezen, OHG. iosan, G. frieren, Icel. frjsa, Sw. frysa, Dan. fryse, Goth. frius cold, frost, and prob. to L. prurire to itch, E. prurient, cf. L. prna a burning coal, pruina hoarfrost, Skr. prushva ice, prush to spirt. Frost.

freight.etymology: F. fret, OHG. fr merit, reward. See Fraught, n.

french.etymology: AS. frencisc, LL. franciscus, from L. Francus a Frank: cf. OF. franceis, franchois, fran, F. franFrank, a., and cf. Frankish.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

frenzy.etymology: OE. frenesie, fransey, F. frénésie, L. phrenesis, fr. Gr. Frantic, Phrenitis.

frequency.etymology: L. frequentia numerous attendance, multitude: cf. F. fréquence. See Frequent.

frequent.etymology: L. frequens, -entis, crowded, frequent, akin to farcire to stuff: cf. F. fréquent. Cf. Farce, n.

fresco.etymology: It., fr. fresco fresh; of German origin. See Fresh, a.

fresh.etymology: OE. fresch, AS. fersc; akin to D. versch, G. frisch, OHG. frisc, Sw. frisk, Dan. frisk, fersk, Icel. fr frisky, brisk, ferskr fresh; cf. It. fresco, OF. fres, freis, fem. freske, fresche, F. frais, fem. fra, which are of German origin. Cf. Fraischeur, Fresco, Frisk.

freshet.etymology: OE. fresche flood + -et. See Fresh, a.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix with a diminutive force; as in baronet, pocket, facet, floweret, latchet.

fret.etymology: OE. freten to eat, consume; AS. fretan, for foretan; pref. for- + etan to eat; akin to D. vreten, OHG. frezzan, G. fressen, Sw. fräta, Goth. fra-itan. See For, and Eat, v. t.

roots.meaning: A prefix to verbs, having usually the force of a negative or privative. It often implies also loss, detriment, or destruction, and sometimes it is intensive, meaning utterly, quite thoroughly, as in forbathe.

friar.etymology: OR. frere, F. frère brother, friar, fr. L. frater brother. See Brother.

fricassee.etymology: F. fricassée, fr. fricasser to fry, fricassee; cf. LL. fricare, perh. for frictare, fricare, frictum, to rub. Cf. Fry, Friction.

friction.etymology: L. frictio, fr. fricare, frictum,to rub: cf. F. friction. See Fray to rub, arid cf. Dentifrice.

friday.etymology: AS. frigedæg, fr. Frigu, the gooddes of marriage; friqu love + dæg day; cf. Icel. Frigg name of a goddess, the wife of Odin or Wodan, OHG. Friatag, Isel. Frjadagr. AS. frigu is prob. from the root of E. friend, free. See Free, and Day.

fridge.etymology: AS. frician to dance, from free bold. Cf. Freak, n.

friend.etymology: From Middle English freend , frend , frende , freynde , friend , frind , frond , frund , vrend , vryend , from Old English frēond , frīond ( “ friend ” , literally “ loving [one], lover ” ) , from Proto-West Germanic *friund , from Proto-Germanic *frijōndz ( “ friend, loved one ” ) , from Proto-Indo-European *preyH- ( “ to please; to love ” ) , roughly equivalent to free +‎ -nd . See also Friday .

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting state, office, dignity, profession, or art; as in lordship, friendship, chancellorship, stewardship, horsemanship.

frieze.etymology: Perh. the same word as frieze a, kind of cloth. Cf. Friz.

frigate.etymology: F. frégate, It. fregata, prob. contracted fr. L. fabricata something constructed or. built. See Fabricate.

fright.etymology: OE. frigt, freyht, AS. fyrhto, fyrhtu; akin to OS. forhta, OHG. forhta, forahta, G. furcht, Dan. frygt, Sw. fruktan, Goth. faúrhtei fear, faúrhts timid.

frigid.etymology: L. frigidus, fr. frigere to be cold; prob. akin to Gr. Frill.

frigorific.etymology: L. frigorificus; frigus, frigoris, cold + facere to make: cf. F. frigorifique.

frill.etymology: OF. friller, fr. L. frigidulus somewhat cold, dim. of frigidus cold; akin to F. frileux chilly.

fringe.etymology: OF, fringe, F. frange, prob. fr. L. fimbria fiber, thread, fringe, cf. fibra fiber, E. fiber, fimbriate.

fringilla.etymology: NL., fr. L. fringilla a chaffinch.

frippery.etymology: F. friperie, fr. fruper. See Fripper.

frisk.etymology: OF. frieque, cf. OHG. frise lively, brisk, fresh, Dan. & Sw. frisk, Icel. friskr. See Fresh, a.

fritillaria.etymology: NL., fr. L. fritillus dicebox: cf. F. fritillaire. So named from the checkered markings of the petals.

fritter.etymology: OR. fritour, friture, pancake, F. friture frying, a thing fried, from frire to fry. See Far, v. t.

frivolous.etymology: L. frivolus; prob. akin to friare to rub, crumble, E. friable: cf. F. frivole.

frock.etymology: F. froc a monk's cowl, coat, garment, LL. frocus, froccus, flocus, floccus, fr. L. floccus a flock of wool; hence orig., a flocky cloth or garment;cf. L. flaccus flabby, E. flaccid.

frog.etymology: AS. froggu, frocga a frog (in sensel); akin to D. vorsch, OHG. frosk, G. frosch, Icel. froskr, fraukr, Sw. & Dan. frö.

frolic.etymology: D. vroolijk; akin to G. frölich, fr. froh, OHG. fr, Dan. fro, OS. fr, cf. Icel. fr swift; all perh. akin to Skr. pru to spring up.

frond.etymology: L. frons, frondis, a leafy branch, foliage.

front.etymology: F. frant forehead, L. frons, frontis; perh. akin to E. brow.

frontier.etymology: F. frontière, LL. frontaria. See Front.

frontispiece.etymology: F. frontispice, LL. frontispicium beginning, front of a church, fr. L. frons front + spicere, specere, to look at, view: cf. It. frontispizio. See Front and Spy.

frontlet.etymology: OF. frontelet brow band, dim. of frontel, frontal. See Frontal, n.

frost.etymology: OE. frost, forst, AS. forst, frost. fr. freósan to freeze; akin to D. varst, G., OHG., Icel., Dan., & Sw. frost. *18. See Freeze, v. i.

froth.etymology: OE. frothe, Icel. frotha; akin to Dan. fraade, Sw. fradga, AS. afreothan to froth.

froward.etymology: Fro + -ward. See Fro, and cf. Fromward.

roots.meaning: Suffixes denoting course or direction to; motion or tendency toward; as in backward, or backwards; toward, or towards, etc.

frown.etymology: OF. froignier, F. frogner, in se refrogner, se renfrogner, to knit the brow, to frown; perh. of Teutonic origin; cf. It. in frigno wrinkled, frowning, Prov. It. frignare to cringe the face, to make a wry face, dial. Sw. fryna to make a wry face,

fructify.etymology: F. fructifier, L. fructificare; fructus fruit + ficare (only in comp.), akin to L. facere to make. See Fruit, and Fact.

frugal.etymology: L. frugalis, fr. frugi, lit., for fruit; hence, fit for food, useful, proper, temperate, the dative of frux, frugis, fruit, akin to E. fruit: cf. F. frugal. See Fruit, n.

fruit.etymology: OE. fruit, frut, F. fruit, from L. fructus enjoyment, product, fruit, from frui, p. p. fructus, to enjoy; akin to E. brook, v. t. See Broook, v. t., and cf. Fructify, Frugal.

fruition.etymology: OF. fruition, L. fruitio, enjoyment, fr. L. frui, p. p. fruitus, to use or enjoy. See Fruit, n.

frumenty.etymology: OF. fromentée, fr. L. frumentum. See Frumentaceous.

frump.etymology: Cf. Prov. E. frumple to wrinkle, ruffle, D. frommelen.

frustrate.etymology: L. frustratus, p. p. of frustrare, frustrari, to deceive, frustrate, fr. frustra in vain, witout effect, in erorr, prob. for frudtra and akin to fraus, E. fraud.

fruticose.etymology: L. fruticosus, from frutex, fruticis, shrub

fruticulose.etymology: Dim. fr. L. fruticosus bushy: cf. F. fruticuleux.

fry.etymology: OE. frien, F. frire, fr. L. frigere to roast, parch, fry, cf. Gr. bhrajj. Cf. Fritter.

fuchsia.etymology: NL. Named after Leonard Fuchs, a German botanist.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

fucus.etymology: L. rock lichen, orchil, used as a red dye, red or purple color, disguise, deceit.

fuddle.etymology: Perh. formed as a kind of dim. of full. Cf. Fuzzle.

fudge.etymology: Cf. Prov. F. fuche, feuche, an interj. of contempt.

fuel.etymology: OF. fouail, fuail, or fouaille, fuaille, LL. focalium, focale, fr. L. focus hearth, fireplace, in LL., fire. See Focus.

fugacious.etymology: L. fugax, fugacis, from fugere: cf. F. fugace. See Fugitive.

fugitive.etymology: OE. fugitif, F. fugitif, fr. L. fugitivus, fr. fugere to flee. See Bow to bend, and cf. Feverfew.

fugleman.etymology: G. flügelmann file leader; flügel wing (akin to E. fly) + mann man. Cf. Flugrelman.

fugue.etymology: F., fr. It. fuga, fr. L. fuga a fleeing, flight, akin to fugere to fiee. See Fugitive.

fulcrum.etymology: L., bedpost, fr. fulcire to prop.

fulfill.etymology: OE. fulfillen, fulfullen, AS. fulfyllan; ful full + fyllan to fill. See Full, a., and Fill, v. t.

fulgent.etymology: L. fulgens, -entis, p. pr. of fulgere to flash, glitter, shine, akin to Gr. Phlox, Flagrant.

fulgurant.etymology: L. fulgurans, p. pr. of fulgurare.

full.etymology: OE. & AS. ful; akin to OS. ful, D. vol, OHG. fol, G. voll, Icel. fullr, Sw. full, Dan. fuld, Goth. fulls, L. plenus, Gr. p, pr to fill, also to Gr. poly-, pref., G. viel, AS. fela. sq. root80. Cf. Complete, Fill, Plenary, Plenty.

roots.meaning: A combining form or prefix from Gr. poly`s, many; as, polygon, a figure of many angles; polyatomic, having many atoms; polychord, polyconic.

fuller.etymology: AS. fullere, fr. L. fullo. See Full, v. t.

fulmar.etymology: Icel. fulmar. See foul, and Man a gull.

fulminant.etymology: L. fulminans, p. pr. of fulminare to lighten: cf. F. fulminant.

fulminate.etymology: L. fulminatus, p. p. of fulminare to lighten, strike with lightning, fr. fulmen thunderbolt, fr. fulgere to shine. See Fulgent, and cf. Fulmine.

fulmination.etymology: L. fulminatio a darting of lightning: cf. F. fulmination.

roots.meaning: An adjective suffix having primarily the sense of like or same, and indicating a considerable degree of the thing or quality denoted in the first part of the compound; as in mettlesome, full of mettle or spirit; gladsome, full of gladness; winsome, blithesome, etc.

fumble.etymology: Akin to D. fommelen to crumple, fumble, Sw. fumla to fusuble, famla to grope, Dan. famle to grope, fumble, Icel. falme, AS. folm palm of the hand. See Feel, and cf. Fanble, Palm.

fume.etymology: L. fumus; akin to Skr. dh smoke, dh to shake, fan a flame, cf. Gr. fum smoke, F. fumée. Cf. Dust, n., Femerell, Thyme.

fumigant.etymology: L. fumigans, p. pr. of fumigare. See Fumigate.

fumigate.etymology: L. fumigate, p. p. of fumigare to fumigate, fr. fumus smoke. See Fume, n.

fumitory.etymology: OE. fumetere, F. fumeterre, prop., smoke of the ground, fr. L. fumus smoke + terra earth. See Fume, and Terrace.

fun.etymology: Perh. of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. & Gael. fonn pleasure.

function.etymology: L. functio, fr. fungi to perform, execute, akin to Skr. bhuj to enjoy, have the use of: cf. F. fonction. Cf. Defunct.

fund.etymology: OF. font, fond, nom. fonz, bottom, ground, F. fond bottom, foundation, fonds fund, fr. L. fundus bottom, ground, foundation, piece of land. See Found to establish.

fundament.etymology: OE. fundament, fundement, fondement, OF. fundement, fondement, F. fondement, fr. L. fundamentum foundation, fr. fundare to lay the bottom, to found, fr. fundus bottom. See Fund.

funeral.etymology: LL. funeralia, prop. neut. pl. of funeralis of a funeral, fr. L. funus, funeris, funeral: cf. F. funérailles.

funereal.etymology: L. funereus, fr. fentus a funeral.

fungia.etymology: NL., fr. L. fungus mushroom: cf. F. fongie.

fungicide.etymology: Fungi + -cide, fr. L. caedere to kill.

fungus.etymology: L., a mushroom; perh. akin to a doubtful Gr. sponge.

funicle.etymology: L. funiculus, dim. of funis cord, rope: cf. F. funicule funicle (in sense 2). Cf. Funambulo.

funiculus.etymology: L., a little cord. See Funicle.

funk.etymology: OE. funke a little fire; akin to Prov. E. funk touchwood, G. funke spark, and perh. to Goth. f fire.

funnel.etymology: OE. funel, fonel, prob. through OF. fr, L. fundibulum, infundibulum, funnel, fr. infundere to pour in; in in + fundere to pour; cf. Armor. founil funnel, W. ffynel air hole, chimney. See Fuse, v. t.

fur.etymology: OE. furre, OF. forre, fuerre, sheatth, case, of German origin; cf. OHG. fuotar lining, case, G. futter; akin to Icel. f lining, Goth. f, scabbard; cf. Skr. p vessel, dish. The German and Icel. words also have the sense, fodder, but this was probably a different word originally. Cf. Fodder food, Fother, v. t., Forel, n.

furbelow.etymology: Prov. F. farbala, equiv. to F. falbala, It. falbalà.

furbish.etymology: OE. forbischen, OF. forbir, furbir, fourbir, F. fourbir, fr. OHG. furban to clean. See -ish.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to from adjectives from nouns and from adjectives. It denotes relation, resemblance, similarity, and sometimes has a diminutive force; as, selfish, boyish, brutish; whitish, somewhat white.

furcula.etymology: L., a forked prop, dim. of furca a fork.

furious.etymology: L. furiosus, fr. furia rage, fury: cf. F. furieux. See Fury.

furl.etymology: Contr. fr. furdle, fr. fardel bundle: cf. F. ferler to furl, OF. fardeler to pack. See Furdle, Fardel, and cf. Farl.

furlong.etymology: OE. furlong, furlang, AS. furlang, furlung, prop., the length of a furrow; furh furrow + lang long. See Furrow, and Long, a.

furlough.etymology: Prob. fr. D. verlof, fr. a prefix akin to E. for + the root of E. lief, and akin to Dan. forlov, Sw. förlof, G. verlaub permission. See Life, a.

furnace.etymology: OE. fornais, forneis, OF. fornaise, F. fournaise, from L. fornax; akin to furnus oven, and prob. to E. forceps.

furnish.etymology: OF. furnir, fornir, to furnish, finish, F. fournir; akin to Pr. formir, furmir, fromir, to accomplish, satisfy, fr. OHG. frumjan to further, execute, do, akin to E. frame. See Frame, v. t., and - ish.

furniture.etymology: F. fourniture. See Furnish, v. t.

furrow.etymology: OE. forow, forgh, furgh, AS. furh; akin to D. voor, OHG. furuh, G. furche, Dan. fure, Sw. f, Icel. for drain, L. porca ridge between two furrows.

further.etymology: A comparative of forth; OE. further, forther, AS. fur, far; akin to G. fürder. See Forth, adv.

furtive.etymology: L. furtivus, fr. furtum theft, fr. fur thief, akin to ferre to bear: cf. F. furtif. See Fertile.

furuncle.etymology: L. furunculus a petty thief, a boil, dim. of fur thief: cf. F. furoncle.

fusain.etymology: F., the spindle tree; also, charcoal made from it.

fuse.etymology: L. fusus, p. p. of fundere to pour, melt, cast. See Foundo to cast, and cf. Futile.

fusee.etymology: See 2d Fusil, and cf. Fuse, n.

fusible.etymology: F. fusible. See Fuse, v. t.

fusiform.etymology: L. fusus spindle + -form: cf. F. fusiforme.

fusil.etymology: L. fusilis molten, fluid, fr. fundere, fusum, to pour, cast. See Fuse, v. t.

fusillade.etymology: F. fusillade, cf. It. fucilata. See Fusil a firelock.

fusion.etymology: L. fusio, fr. fundere, fusum to pour, melt: cf. F. fusion. See Fuse, v. t., aud cf, Foison.

fustian.etymology: OE. fustan, fustian, OF. fustaine, F. futaine, It. fustagno, fr. LL. fustaneum, fustanum; cf. Pr. fustani, Sp. fustan. So called from Fustat, i. e., Cairo, where it was made.

fustigate.etymology: L. fustigare, fr. fustis stick. See 1st Fust.

futile.etymology: L. futilis that easily pours out, that easily lets loose, vain, worthless, from the root of fundere to pour out: cf. F. futile. See Fuse, v. t.

future.etymology: F. futur, L. futurus, used as fut. p. of esse to be, but from the same root as E. be. See Be, v. i.

fuzz.etymology: Cf. Prov. E. fuzzy that ravels (of silk or cotton), D. voos spongy, fungous, G. faser filament. E. feaze to untwist.
